analysis.one_liner: Keeps retired coal miners' health benefits funded by shifting surplus pension money and charging companies that leave the plan.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a Democrat with four Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it arrived and never received a vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill aimed to guarantee that retired United Mine Workers members and their dependents keep receiving health benefits from the union's 1950 and 1974 Benefit Plans. It would move any surplus money in the miners' pension plan into the underfunded health plans, and it would make large coal companies that leave the plans pay their share of the plans' unfunded obligations. It also directed federal health officials to impose managed care and cost-control rules on the plans so benefits stay affordable.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired United Mine Workers members and their dependents who depend on the 1950 and 1974 Benefit Plans for health coverage, whose benefits would be shored up with excess pension assets and protected by withdrawal charges and guaranteed employer contribution rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired coal miners and their dependents

how_it_helps.text: Transfers any excess assets in the UMWA 1950 Pension Plan — money beyond what is needed to pay accrued pensions — into the underfunded 1950 and 1974 health benefit plans, based on each plan's deficit.

Establishes withdrawal liability for coal companies that produced or processed more than 300,000 tons under the 1988 wage agreement and are signatories, so a company cannot simply exit the health plans and leave retirees' costs behind.

Requires the union and the Bituminous Coal Operators' Association to set employer contribution rates sufficient to prevent plan deficits, with the Secretary of Labor stepping in to assess and collect from employers if they fail to do so.

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue binding cost-containment rules — drug formularies, physician payment limits, utilization review — with the primary goal of quality care at or below medical price inflation, to keep the plans solvent without cutting the basic promise.

analysis.who_pays: Large coal companies that are signatories to the 1988 wage agreement would owe withdrawal liability if they exit the plans and would be locked into guaranteed contribution rates; physicians, hospitals, and drug suppliers would face Medicare-allowable payment caps, formularies, and volume discounts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large coal companies and health care providers

drawbacks.text: The cost-containment program would impose cost-sharing, yearly recertification, a drug formulary, and physician payments limited to Medicare allowable charges — so retirees could face more out-of-pocket costs and tighter networks than the plans traditionally offered.

Companies leaving the plans would owe their share of the plans' unfunded obligations in equal monthly installments over 60 months, with default triggering immediate payment of the full outstanding amount plus interest — a significant financial burden on exiting employers.
Diverting excess pension assets to the health plans leaves nothing in reserve if the pension plan's actuarial position deteriorates later, since the transfer is one-way.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: retirees' health coverage gets a stable funding base, paid for by the coal companies that employed them and somewhat trimmed benefits (cost sharing, Medicare-rate physician payments). For the tens of thousands of retired miners and widows whose plans were struggling, that is a favorable trade; the main honest objection is that the withdrawal charges and funding guarantees are heavy obligations for coal companies, and the benefit trims are real for retirees who previously had richer coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. David Boren (D-OK) introduced the bill on April 8, 1992, joined by four Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large coal companies are better off: because the bill died, they face no new withdrawal liability for leaving the retiree health plans and no federally guaranteed funding obligation. The retiree health plans' funding question was left unresolved by this bill.

for.name: Sen. David Boren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shore up funding for UMWA retiree health benefits.

for.name: 4 of 43 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including the Senate Republican leader
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from both parties' leadership.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, never held a markup, and never allowed it a floor vote.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled action on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines at the top: a Democratic senator introduced it and four Republican senators, including the Republican leader, cosponsored it — so the bill died in a committee rather than on a partisan floor vote.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies (signatories to the 1988 wage agreement)
industries.note: The bill would charge them their share of the health plans' unfunded obligations when they withdraw and lock them into guaranteed contribution rates, keeping them permanently on the hook for retiree benefits. Blocking the bill preserved their ability to shed those legacy obligations.

The bill directs federal rules capping physician payments at Medicare allowable charges, imposing drug formularies, and extracting volume discounts — reducing payments from the plans. Their interest in cheaper care runs against the plans' cost of providing it.
The plans would receive excess pension assets and guaranteed employer funding, directly shoring up the health coverage retired miners depend on.
